Following random allocation, half of the participants were told that they would have the option to cash out their bets before the outcome of the sports event is known, while the other half did not have this option.
During some trials, participants were offered a "cash-out" option for a partial payout based on the expected value of their wager.

To ensure data quality and validity in the primary analyses, participants were excluded if they (i) were under the age of 18 years, (ii) did not solve at least 7 of the 10 CAPTCHAs correctly, (iii) were self-reportedly under the influence of any drugs or alcohol during the experiment, (iv) did not demonstrate understanding the cash-out feature, (v) failed the attention check, (vi) completed the survey in less than three minutes, or (vii) provided the same answer on ten consecutive survey items.
Further participants were removed from analysis due to incomplete survey responses (n = 35), invariant responding across ≥10 items (n = 35), and completion times under three minutes (n = 2).
After applying all preregistered and adjusted exclusion criteria, the final analytic sample consisted of 595 participants.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The minimum target sample size was determined in consultation with the recruiting partner, Vegas.hu. Based on their prior experience with the availability of eligible participants, they estimated that at least 500 valid responses could be obtained with high certainty after applying exclusions. Therefore, this number was treated as the minimum guaranteed recruitment sample size. A power analysis using the pwr package in R determined that 500 participants would provide evidence for an effect size of 0.23 (Pearson r) in a regression model with 43 predictors (Team R, 2013) at a 0.05 significance level with 0.80 power for testing H1 (see next section for study hypotheses). Based on a prior randomized online experiment (see Study 3 by Newall et al. [2022], using a similar strategy), it was estimated that approximately 61% of these participants would place bets, resulting in a subset of 305 participants for testing H2 and H3 (see next section for study hypotheses). A power analysis suggested that this subset would provide statistical evidence for an effect size of 0.29 (Pearson r) under the same statistical conditions. Such an effect size estimate is consistent with the upper bound of effect sizes found in recent meta-analyses on related phenomena. For instance, a meta-analysis of pop-up interventions during gambling (Bjørseth et al., 2021) found an overall effect size of g = 0.507 (approximately r = .25). Similarly, a meta-analysis on gambling advertisements and their impact on gambling behavior (Bouguettaya et al., 2020) reported effect sizes ranging from r = -.08 to r = .68. However, because no prior research has used experimental methods to directly estimate the present effect, there are no studies that could be directly used to estimate the expected magnitude of the effect.

Based on the 500 minimum target sample size mentioned above, we expect 305 participants to place a bet. Power analysis determined that this would provide evidence for an effect size of r = 0.29.

It was also likely that a substantially larger sample than 500 participants could be recruited by the gaming partner (Vegas.hu). Therefore, to avoid unnecessarily wasting participants' time, the smallest effect sizes of interest were identified. It was considered that an effect of r = 0.1 would still be of theoretical and practical interest. The sample size required to detect such an effect (at α = .05 with 80% power) was calculated. This resulted in a sample size of 2,840 participants. For that reason, if possible, the plan was to continue data collection up to 2,840 participants for H2 and H3. Data collection would cease if either (i) this upper recruitment limit was reached or (ii) Vegas.hu exhausted its pool of potential gamblers to contact.

live_data_statements: Following random allocation, half of the participants were told that they would have the option to cash out their bets before the outcome of the sports event is known, while the other half did not have this option.
During some trials, participants were offered a "cash-out" option for a partial payout based on the expected value of their wager.
Participants completed the study online.

During recruitment, participants were informed of a payment structure consisting of 3,000 HUF + 2,300 HUF + 700 HUF for completing specific tasks, for a total compensation of 6,000 HUF. 1During the experiment, they were told that they could receive 2,300 HUF by decoding randomly generated sequences of letters and numbers from distorted images (i.e., CAPTCHAs).
At the end of the study, participants were debriefed about the purpose of the study and that their bets were simulated.
Participants were then prompted with an attention check question, followed by an exclusion question asking if they are under the influence of drugs or alcohol (yes/no).
Following this task, half of the participants were randomly assigned to the cash-out condition, while the other half were randomly assigned to the no-cash-out condition.

The only difference between the two groups was that in the cash-out condition, participants were informed about the option to cash out the following way: "If you place a bet, after placing the bet, before and during the sporting event, you will have the possibility to use the cash-out function to collect your winnings (see Experiment Flow Diagram)."
Participants were then redirected to the webpage where they could choose to place their bet.
All participants were given instructions on how they could make their bets.
Below these options, participants were able to manually enter the amount of money they wanted to wager.

1 The list of sports events depended on the available events at the gambling website during data collection, and only events that were scheduled to occur after participants completed the questionnaire and betting task were offered.

First, participants were shown a large collection of sports events that would take place in the target two-week period, therefore participants' experiences closely resembled their real-life gambling experiences.
Second, participants were given realistic odds for each of the outcomes as calculated by a gambling service provider.

After participants had placed their bet or chosen not to bet, they were asked to fill out a self-report survey comprising three sections: demographic measures, measures that might moderate the effect of the cash-out option on gambling behavior, and a question assessing understanding of the cash-out option (see section on 'Self-report measures').
Finally, participants were offered the contact details of professionals who could help them in case they felt they needed help with any gambling-related problems.
assessed using two questions: (i) attention check (participants were presented with the following item: "This question is designed to test participants' attentiveness.

This item was a modified item from Paas and Morren (2018); and (ii) under the influence (participants were asked "Are you currently under the influence of mindaltering substances (e.g., drugs or alcohol)?"

Demographic measures: Various demographic information was collected (adapted from Szecsi et al. [2024]) including (i) age (participants were requested to select their birth year from a dropdown list); (ii) employment status (participants were requested to specify their current primary employment status: "Full-time (not entrepreneur)", "Part-time", "Entrepreneur", "Unemployed", "Retired", "Other").
Dummy variables were created using 'Full-time (not entrepreneur)" and "Other" as reference groups; (iii) gender (participants were asked to indicate their gender.

Following the official measure of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD; 2023) for household income, the measure was transformed by dividing it by the square root of the number of household members, in order to adjust for the number of individuals using the income; (v) highest educational attainment (participants were asked to indicate their highest completed educational level: "Less than elementary school", "Elementary school", "Skilled worker qualification", "High school", "Vocational education", "BA/BSc", "MA/MSc", "Doctorate or higher").

Helmert codes were used for this variable in the analysis; (vi) number of household members (participants were asked to indicate the total number of individuals in their household, including themselves).
Experience with the cash-out feature: Participants were asked "Have you had any prior experience with the cash-out function".
As aforementioned, participants were recruited via the mailing list of the Hungarian online gambling service provider, Vegas.hu.
A total of 1,126 participants were recruited for the study.

To ensure data quality and validity in the primary analyses, participants were excluded if they (i) were under the age of 18 years, (ii) did not solve at least 7 of the 10 CAPTCHAs correctly, (iii) were self-reportedly under the influence of any drugs or alcohol during the experiment, (iv) did not demonstrate understanding the cash-out feature, (v) failed the attention check, (vi) completed the survey in less than three minutes, or (vii) provided the same answer on ten consecutive survey items.
Further participants were removed from analysis due to incomplete survey responses (n = 35), invariant responding across ≥10 items (n = 35), and completion times under three minutes (n = 2).
After applying all preregistered and adjusted exclusion criteria, the final analytic sample consisted of 595 participants.

To test whether participants were more likely to place bets in the cash-out condition (H1), the registered intention-to-treat binomial logistic regression models were fitted to predict whether participants chose to make a bet or not.

Participants may not have treated the reward as equivalent to their own money, although the CAPTCHA reward was framed as money participants had personally earned to strengthen their sense of ownership over it.
Only 20 participants had no prior experience with the feature (3%).

Another possibility behind the null findings involves the number of betting decisions participants were asked to make. Bennett et al. (2024) used repeated trials, and they found that the effect of cash-out on bet amount was initially small and increased over repeated bet decisions.
Participants were likely to be familiar with the feature and have their own experiences and interpretations of the feature that the present study's explanation could not override.

Finally, longitudinal designs where participants are introduced to the cash-out feature and their betting behaviors are tracked over time may provide insight into the long-term impact of the cash-out feature.
Consequently, the research team identified those cases where at least 10% of the participants provided the same alternative response to one CAPTCHA letter, and these were accepted as correct.

Participants were categorized into four categories (i.e., no-risk, low-risk, moderate-risk, and problem gambler) according to the scoring guide of the PGSI, and the Helmert-coded 3 version of it was used in the regression analysis.

text.text: The rise of online sports betting, facilitated by technological innovations such as the cash-out feature, has transformed the gambling landscape.

While cash-outs (a facility provided by betting operators which allows gamblers to close a bet early before the final outcome of a sports event is known) have been suggested to intensify problematic gambling behaviors, empirical studies to date have been correlational, leaving a gap in determining causal evidence.
The present Registered Report investigated the direct impact of the perceived availability of the cash-out feature on various facets of gambling behavior in an online experiment.
Hungarian residents with an online gambling history (N=595) were informed that they would have the chance to gamble with real money on sports events.

Following random allocation, half of the participants were told that they would have the option to cash out their bets before the outcome of the sports event is known, while the other half did not have this option.
Overall, the findings provided evidence that cash-out availability did not influence bet placement, wager size, or bet risk among our sample.
However, the low variance in the outcomes may have limited the ability to detect subtle differences.
Consequently, the null results should not be taken as conclusive evidence of no behavioral effect.
Online sports betting has significantly increased in recent decades, with the number of users worldwide projected to reach 314.5 million players by 2030 (Statista, 2026).
text.formatted: Online sports betting has significantly increased in recent decades, with the number of users worldwide projected to reach 314.5 million players by 2030 <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Statista, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This popularity can be partly attributed to the introduction of cash-outs, a facility provided by betting operators which allows gamblers to close a bet early before the final outcome of a sports event is known.
While cash-outs provide bettors with an additional decision point during gambling, their impact on betting behavior remains unclear.
Much of prior research has focused on inplay betting more broadly, highlighting its association with a greater risk of harm (Hing et al., 2016 (Hing et al., , 2017;; Killick & Griffiths, 2019).

text.text: For example, a British gambling prevalence study (Gambling Commission, 2018) reported that the proportion of gamblers classified as problem gamblers was much higher among those who bet in-play compared to online gamblers who do not (27.4% vs.

text.text: However, in-play betting is a broader concept than cash-outs because it refers to bettors' ability to place, adjust, or close bets while a sporting event is ongoing.
Prior studies have not isolated the specific role of cash-outs in gambling behavior and have used correlational designs.
The present study aimed to bridge this gap by conducting an online experiment.

The study investigated several dimensions of betting behavior, including the proportion of participants placing bets, bet sizes, and bet risks, both in the presence and the absence of cash-out options.
Importantly, the study also examined the differential effects on specific high-risk subgroups.

Ever since the British gambling operator William Hill first introduced cash-outs in 2012 (Gaming Intelligence, 2014), they have become a common feature on online sports betting sites (Killick & Griffiths, 2019; Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2016).
text.formatted: Ever since the British gambling operator William Hill first introduced cash-outs in 2012 (Gaming Intelligence, 2014), they have become a common feature on online sports betting sites <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Killick & Griffiths, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The increased penetration of smartphones and the 'always-on' culture have significantly facilitated this trend, increasing the availability of gambling, which has important implications for bettors' decision-making (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019; Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017).
text.formatted: The increased penetration of smartphones and the 'always-on' culture have significantly facilitated this trend, increasing the availability of gambling, which has important implications for bettors' decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: There are different forms of cash-out, including full cash-out, partial cash-out (only part of the bet is cashed out), and automatic cash-out (if at any point during an event, the cash-out value matches a preset amount, the bet is automatically cashed out).

Similar to other bets, the amount offered for the cash-out is calculated by the gambling provider based on several factors, including the odds and amount of the original bet, as well as how the given event is progressing.
For example, if the home team scores a goal in a football match, their odds of winning increase, resulting in an increased cash-out offer to players compared to before the goal was scored.
The mere availability of cash-outs for sports events can have important implications even if nobody cashes out their bet, because it can influence key decisions during gambling.
For instance, it could impact how many individuals bet, how much money they wager, and the level of risk in their betting.
One key cognitive heuristic by which cash-outs influence gambling behaviors is the illusion of control (Langer, 1975) it creates.
text.formatted: One key cognitive heuristic by which cash-outs influence gambling behaviors is the illusion of control <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Langer, 1975)</ref> it creates.

text.text: By offering the option to close bets early, cashouts can -falsely -increase the perceived control over the success of the bets even though the objective level of control over the final success of the bets remains unchanged.

Therefore, cashouts can nudge players to take greater risks by giving them the impression that they can close their bets with minimal losses. Bennett et al. (2024) demonstrated this effect by utilizing a cardbetting task (Bennett, 2022).
text.formatted: Therefore, cashouts can nudge players to take greater risks by giving them the impression that they can close their bets with minimal losses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bennett et al. (2024)</ref> demonstrated this effect by utilizing a cardbetting task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bennett, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this task, participants predicted the color of a randomly selected card (red or blue) from 10 cards, and participants could wager points on each prediction.
During some trials, participants were offered a "cash-out" option for a partial payout based on the expected value of their wager.
The authors found that participants' bet amounts increased by up to 35% when the cash-out option was available.
They posited that the perception of the initial bet being reversible may have increased their perception of control over the outcome.
Consequently, this perceived control could appeal to inexperienced or low-risk gamblers, increasing their risk tolerance as an effect of the greater perception of control.

Similarly, Lopez-Gonzalez and Griffiths (2017) suggested that the cash-out feature can potentially increase the vulnerability of the bettors, because they can view gambling on sports as an investment, such as trading on the stock market, where they can control when to open and close their positions.
text.formatted: Similarly, Lopez-Gonzalez and <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Griffiths (2017)</ref> suggested that the cash-out feature can potentially increase the vulnerability of the bettors, because they can view gambling on sports as an investment, such as trading on the stock market, where they can control when to open and close their positions.

text.text: Moreover, some sports betting advertisements appear to encourage gamblers to see themselves as professionals by promoting game analysis to beat the service providers (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2018). Parke and Parke (2019) conducted an observational study on 19 online sports bettors with problematic gaming patterns and noted that the cash-out feature was associated with prolonged online sports betting sessions and increased bet frequency by enabling bettors to rapidly re-stake the cashed-out money, reinforcing impulsive and continuous gambling behaviors while minimizing breaks.

text.text: Enabling bettors to cash-out changes the structure of betting from a previously discontinuous form of gambling (placing a single bet on the sporting event's final outcome) into a continuous one (i.e., bettors can now make multiple bets during a sporting event on many different aspects as opposed to placing a single bet on the winner) (Griffiths & Auer, 2013; Harris & Griffiths, 2018). Hing et al. (2016) similarly reported that a higher frequency of bet placements and impulsive responses to betting opportunities, such as the use of the cash-out feature, was associated with a higher risk of harm from gambling.

(2016)</ref> similarly reported that a higher frequency of bet placements and impulsive responses to betting opportunities, such as the use of the cash-out feature, was associated with a higher risk of harm from gambling.

text.text: Self-report survey-based studies (Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017; Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019) have suggested that the use of cash-out functions is more prevalent among problem gamblers.
text.formatted: Self-report survey-based studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019)</ref> have suggested that the use of cash-out functions is more prevalent among problem gamblers.

text.text: While these studies offer valuable insights into the gamblers' psychological and demographic attributes (e.g., perceptions, clinical characteristics, income) and their offline gambling activities, they only provide correlational evidence.

Moreover, it is not clear whether (i) the availability of cash-out in sports betting increases problem gambling, (ii) problem gamblers are more prone to play more impulsively when cash-out options are readily available, or (iii) the relationship is bidirectional.
While cash-outs are often discussed within the broader context of in-play betting, they also function as a standalone feature, yet research isolating their effects remains scarce.
Most prior studies have largely focused on in-play betting as a whole, emphasizing its continuous nature and association with problem gambling.

For example, behavioral tracking data (LaBrie et al., 2007; LaPlante et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 2008) and self-report studies (Hing et al., 2016 (Hing et al., , 2017;; Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017) have associated in-play betting with higher gambling risk.
text.formatted: For example, behavioral tracking data <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(LaBrie et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">LaPlante et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Nelson et al., 2008)</ref> and self-report studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hing et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hing et al., , 2017;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lopez-Gonzalez & Griffiths, 2017)</ref> have associated in-play betting with higher gambling risk.

text.text: However, these studies do not distinguish whether the observed risks stem from cash-outs themselves or from other features of in-play betting, such as the ability to place multiple rapid bets within a single event.
Consequently, there is a lack of research specifically isolating the effects of cash-outs on gambling behavior, highlighting the need for experimental research that isolates the effects of cash-outs.
Additionally, the effects of cash-outs may not be uniform across all bettors.

Individual differences, such as financial status (Gray et al., 2012), high trait impulsivity (Hing et al., 2018), and lower statistical numeracy skills (Cokely et al., 2012), have been associated with higher gambling risk.
text.formatted: Individual differences, such as financial status <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gray et al., 2012)</ref>, high trait impulsivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hing et al., 2018)</ref>, and lower statistical numeracy skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cokely et al., 2012)</ref>, have been associated with higher gambling risk.

text.text: Moreover, studies have identified frequent and intensive betting combined with high variability in wagering amounts and an increasing bet size during the first month of actual online gambling to be associated with high-risk subgroups among gamblers (Braverman & Shaffer, 2012), while participating in two different gambling types along with in-play betting has been reported to be an important predictor of gambling problems (Braverman et al., 2013).

text.text: Another study found that while demographic differences in cash-out feature use can be reasonably expected, no significant differences were found in participants' demographicssuch as gender, sexual identity, ethnicity, education, employment status, household income, and relationship status -regarding their use of cash-out features (Sinclair et al., 2024).

text.text: The authors recognized that their sample may have lacked diversity and might not be representative of the general population.
Moreover, while researchers might not observe significant demographic differences in cash-out use, other factors such as bet risk, bet size, or betting behavior may still vary.
Taking this into account, demographics could still play a role in cashout use under different conditions.
Additionally, heterogeneity in the impact of cash-outs may exist due to factors beyond demographics.

While the extant literature provides insight regarding the potential risks and motivations underlying the cash-out feature, a comprehensive understanding of its direct impact on gambling behavior remains elusive.
To date, most studies have been correlational, leaving a gap in determining causal mechanisms.
The present study sought to address this by employing an experimental methodology, offering a more robust examination of the effects of cash-out options.

Moreover, recognizing the potential heterogeneity in responses, the study more deeply examined the differential impacts on specific high-risk subgroups, including those with low income, low numeracy skills, high impulsiveness, or mental health issues.

By doing so, the study aimed to provide a nuanced understanding of the cash-out feature's influence, enriching the literature and offering actionable insights for both policymakers and stakeholders in the gambling industry.
The study was designed as an online experiment to delineate the effect of the perceived availability of the cash-out option on online gambling behavior.

Participants in the cash-out condition were informed that they would have the option cash-out their bets before the event the participant bet on concluded, although in reality, the experiment ended before the actual cash-out could happen.

Such deception was a necessary and crucial part of the study because it addressed the potential hypothetical bias (Harrison, 2024) and ensured that the decision of the gamblers accurately reflected their natural responses to the availability of the cash-out option.

text.text: Participants completed the study online.
All participants who completed the study were paid a total fee of 6,000 Hungarian Forints (HUF) at the end of the experiment.

During recruitment, participants were informed of a payment structure consisting of 3,000 HUF + 2,300 HUF + 700 HUF for completing specific tasks, for a total compensation of 6,000 HUF. 1During the experiment, they were told that they could receive 2,300 HUF by decoding randomly generated sequences of letters and numbers from distorted images (i.e., CAPTCHAs).

text.text: At the end of the study, participants were debriefed about the purpose of the study and that their bets were simulated.
They received a 700 HUF consolation prize for not winning or losing what they thought they had made on the bet, contrary to what they were informed before the experiment began.
After providing informed consent, participants received instructions to avoid any nonexperiment-related activities, such as listening to music or chatting.
Participants were then prompted with an attention check question, followed by an exclusion question asking if they are under the influence of drugs or alcohol (yes/no).
Participants who provided any response to the attention check question or answered 'yes' to the exclusion question were not permitted to continue, and the questionnaire automatically ended for them.
Participants who passed all checks were then informed that if they completed seven or more CAPTCHA codes correctly, they would receive a bonus payment of 2,300 HUF.
The completion of CAPTCHA codes served two purposes.
First, it was used as an attention check.
Participants who failed to complete at least seven of the ten CAPTCHA codes were excluded from the main analyses.
Second, by making participants work for the financial reward, it was expected to increase their sense of ownership of the financial bonus (for a similar approach, see Newall et al. [2022]).

text.text: Following this task, half of the participants were randomly assigned to the cash-out condition, while the other half were randomly assigned to the no-cash-out condition.
Participants in both conditions were told that they could gamble some or all of their financial bonus on one sports game, choosing from a list of potential events, or they could opt not to gamble.

The only difference between the two groups was that in the cash-out condition, participants were informed about the option to cash out the following way: "If you place a bet, after placing the bet, before and during the sporting event, you will have the possibility to use the cash-out function to collect your winnings (see Experiment Flow Diagram)."

text.text: The study used a description of the cash-out feature closely adapted from the Betfair website.
"Cash-out lets you take profit early if your bet is coming in or get some of your stake back if your bet is going against you-all before the event you're betting on is over.
Cash-out offers are made in real time on your current bets, based on live market prices.
Cash-out is available on a wide range of sports, including football, tennis, horse racing, and many more!
You can cash-out of bets pre-play, in-play, and between legs".
Participants were then redirected to the webpage where they could choose to place their bet.
All participants were given instructions on how they could make their bets.
They were told that they could gamble on a sporting event that would take place a few days after they had completed the experiment.

To make the experience of the participants as close as possible to real-life online gambling, the structure and the content of the gambling options followed the commonly used format of online gambling providers in Hungary.
That is, the sporting event was described (e.g., a football [soccer] match: Barcelona vs.
Real Madrid), along with the time and date of the match, the odds for the 'home win', 'away win', and -where relevant -the 'draw' option.
Below these options, participants were able to manually enter the amount of money they wanted to wager.
Participants could only make one bet.
The amount of the bet could not exceed the financial bonus they were given.

To maximize the probability that participants would find the gambling options appealing, they were shown approximately 50-100 sports events that they could bet on covering the following sports: football, handball, rugby, e-sports, ice hockey, American football, boxing, tennis, water polo, basketball, and futsal.

The data regarding gambling events shown in the experiment was extracted from the largest Hungarian online gambling website (www.szerencsejatek.hu) one day before the data collection started and was updated on a 2-to-3-day interval.

This approach yielded two distinct advantages.

First, participants were shown a large collection of sports events that would take place in the target two-week period, therefore participants' experiences closely resembled their real-life gambling experiences.
Second, participants were given realistic odds for each of the outcomes as calculated by a gambling service provider.

After participants had placed their bet or chosen not to bet, they were asked to fill out a self-report survey comprising three sections: demographic measures, measures that might moderate the effect of the cash-out option on gambling behavior, and a question assessing understanding of the cash-out option (see section on 'Self-report measures').
After the experiment, debriefing took place, where the true aim of the study was explained to the participants.
They were also informed that the bets they had made were not real, but they would receive a consolation prize, irrespective of how their bet would have played out.
Finally, participants were offered the contact details of professionals who could help them in case they felt they needed help with any gambling-related problems.

The available options aligned with the Hungarian language, which uses a single term that encompasses both biological and social genders ("Female/Woman", "Male/Man", "I prefer not to answer").

Dummy variables were created using "Male/Man" as the reference group; (iv) household income (participants rated their household's net monthly income on a scale ranging from less than 50,000 HUF [~140 USD] to more than 1,500,000 HUF [~4,100 USD], divided into 30 equal increments, with the final bracket for incomes exceeding 1,500,000 HUF).
Household income was converted by using the midpoint of each income range.
For the highest open-ended category (more than 1,500,000 HUF), they were assigned the value of 1,500,000 HUF 4 .

Following the official measure of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD; 2023) for household income, the measure was transformed by dividing it by the square root of the number of household members, in order to adjust for the number of individuals using the income; (v) highest educational attainment (participants were asked to indicate their highest completed educational level: "Less than elementary school", "Elementary school", "Skilled worker qualification", "High school", "Vocational education", "BA/BSc", "MA/MSc", "Doctorate or higher").

Helmert codes were used for this variable in the analysis; (vi) number of household members (participants were asked to indicate the total number of individuals in their household, including themselves).
To prevent typos, numbers greater than 15 were not permitted.
Experience with the cash-out feature: Participants were asked "Have you had any prior experience with the cash-out function".
Responses were: (1) "I first heard about it in this study"; and (2) "I knew about it before this study".

Understanding cash-out: To see whether participants who were assigned to the cashout condition had a sufficient understanding of the cash-out feature, they were asked to choose the correct description of cash-outs from four different options (see Appendix).

Reliability and validity of self-report measures: To assess the reliability of the selfreport measures used (BIS-R-21, PGSI-HU, and Berlin Numeracy Test), Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega for each measure were calculated to assess internal consistency and Item Response Theory analysis was conducted for the Berlin Numeracy Test to evaluate item difficulty, discrimination, and model fit.
The correlations between self-report measures were examined for construct validity.
Criterion validity was assessed by comparing participants' scores on self-report measures with betting behaviors observed during the task.

More specifically, correlations between all self-report measures and behavioral outcomes -including (i) whether or not the participants place a bet, (ii) the bet amount. and (iii) the odds ratio of the bets placed -were analyzed.
Significant correlations supported the criterion validity of these self-report measures.

It was also likely that a substantially larger sample than 500 participants could be recruited by the gaming partner (Vegas.hu).
Therefore, to avoid unnecessarily wasting participants' time, the smallest effect sizes of interest were identified.
It was considered that an effect of r = 0.1 would still be of theoretical and practical interest.
The sample size required to detect such an effect (at α = .05 with 80% power) was calculated.
This resulted in a sample size of 2,840 participants.
For that reason, if possible, the plan was to continue data collection up to 2,840 participants for H2 and H3.
Data collection would cease if either (i) this upper recruitment limit was reached or (ii) Vegas.hu exhausted its pool of potential gamblers to contact.
In the present study, the impact of the availability of the cash-out option on three dimensions of gambling behavior was investigated.
Accordingly, in the primary confirmatory analyses, three confirmatory hypotheses (Hs) were tested.

It was hypothesized that (i) participants would be more likely to place a bet in the cash-out condition compared to the no cash-out condition (H1); (ii) among participants who placed a bet, individuals would place higher cash amounts in the cash-out condition compared to the no cash-out condition (H2); and (iii) among participants who placed a bet, individuals would select bets with higher odds (riskier bets) in the cash-out condition compared to the no cash-out condition (H3).
To test the robustness of the primary analyses and to test their sensitivity to different analytical choices, a multiverse analysis was conducted.
Moreover, exploratory analyses aimed to identify which factors moderated the effect of cash-out options on gambling behavior.
To do this, random forest models concerning each of the aforementioned hypotheses defined were conducted.
To make inferences, an alpha level of .05 was used.
In case a p-value was significant, and the direction of the interaction aligned with the hypotheses, it was treated as evidence for the hypothesis.

If a p-value was nonsignificant or significant but the direction of the effect was misaligned with the hypotheses, it was concluded that there was no evidence for the existence of the effect, and if the effect existed, the effect size (r) was likely smaller than 0.23 (or 0.1 depending on the final sample size), as determined by the power analysis.
As aforementioned, participants were recruited via the mailing list of the Hungarian online gambling service provider, Vegas.hu.
Individuals who met the criteria of being at least 18 years old, residing in Hungary, and having prior experience in sports betting were eligible to participate.
Vegas.hu sent out recruitment emails in chunks to the participants, and data collection took place from 19 January 2026 to 28 January 2026.
A total of 1,126 participants were recruited for the study.
Individuals who did not provide informed consent or who exited the survey before providing any survey or behavioral data were excluded prior to the application of the exclusion criteria.

To ensure data quality and validity in the primary analyses, participants were excluded if they (i) were under the age of 18 years, (ii) did not solve at least 7 of the 10 CAPTCHAs correctly, (iii) were self-reportedly under the influence of any drugs or alcohol during the experiment, (iv) did not demonstrate understanding the cash-out feature, (v) failed the attention check, (vi) completed the survey in less than three minutes, or (vii) provided the same answer on ten consecutive survey items.
For the 69 participants who failed the attention check, and the 14 who reported being under the influence of alcohol or drugs, the survey immediately ended.
This resulted in an initial analyzable sample of 963 participants.
To ensure response quality, 1 CAPTCHA responses containing numerical characters or incorrect character lengths were classified as incorrect.
Furthermore, the CAPTCHA scoring procedure were modified to account for visually ambiguous characters (See section deviations from preregistration).
1 The adjusted scoring procedures were developed prior to hypothesis testing.
The scoring procedure resulted in the exclusion of 221 participants.
An additional 155 participants, who failed to demonstrate understanding of the cashout feature, were excluded.
Further participants were removed from analysis due to incomplete survey responses (n = 35), invariant responding across ≥10 items (n = 35), and completion times under three minutes (n = 2).
These exclusion categories were not mutually exclusive.
Therefore, exclusion counts do not sum up to the total number of excluded participants.
After applying all preregistered and adjusted exclusion criteria, the final analytic sample consisted of 595 participants.
Of the final sample (N = 595), 80% (n = 474) chose to place a bet and were included in analyses to test H2 and H3.

Internal consistency was acceptable to excellent across self-report measures in the study sample.

To test the primary hypotheses, three sets of analyses were conducted, one for each hypothesis.
In each of these sets, the analysis fitted two separate models, one containing the experimental condition dummy (cash-out vs. no cash-out) and one not.

Both models included the following variables that have been theorized to affect gambling-related behavior: impulsiveness, problem gambling, gaming patterns, numeracy, age, employment, gender, household income divided by the square root of the number of household members, highest educational attainment, and experience with the cash-out feature.

To test whether participants were more likely to place bets in the cash-out condition (H1), the registered intention-to-treat binomial logistic regression models were fitted to predict whether participants chose to make a bet or not.

The results did not support the hypothesis that participants in the cash-out condition would be more likely to place bets compared to participants in the no cash-out condition (OR = 1.00, 95% CI [0.64, 1.58], p = .993).
The addition of the cash-out predictor did not significantly improve the model fit compared to the baseline model (χ 2 (1) < 0.01, p = .993).

text.text: However, it was observed that 80% of participants chose to place a bet, indicating a potential ceiling effect that likely reduced statistical power to detect a difference.

text.text: To test whether participants who placed bets selected bets with higher odds (riskier bets) in the cash-out condition (H3), first, the decimal odds were transformed into probabilities by taking the reciprocal of the odds before the analysis.
This transformation places the decimal odds selected on a probability scale making it more suitable for linear repression analysis.
Then, linear regression models were fitted to predict the probabilities associated with the chosen bets of the individuals.
The effect of the availability of cash-out on bet risk remained non-significant, β = -0.031, 95% CI [-0.066, 0.003], p = .077.

The baseline model, including only covariates, explained 11.5% of the variance of the odds selected by participants (R² = .115), while the model including cash-out and covariates explained 12.1% of the variance (R² = .121), an increase of ΔR² = .006.
The addition of cash-out did not significantly improve the model fit compared to the baseline model, F(1, 435) = 3.14, p = .077.
Therefore, H3 was not supported.
To assess the robustness of the results and their sensitivity against the methodological choices, a multiverse analysis was conducted.
Multiverse analysis involves "performing all analyses across the whole set of alternatively processed data sets corresponding to a large set of reasonable scenarios" (Steegen et al., 2016; p. 702).

The multiverse analysis was exploratory because there were no specific hypotheses for each analysis.
Accordingly, multiple versions of the analyses specified in the primary analysis was conducted with 24 (2 x 12) alternatively processed datasets.
First, all analyses were repeated with the exclusion criteria listed above and also including all individuals without excluding any participant.

Second, all analyses were repeated with 11 different imputation methods: with the imputation listed in the primary analyses, with only the inclusion of complete cases, and with the use of different k values (1-10).
In addition to the analysis of bet risk (H3), a robustness analysis was conducted using untransformed decimal odds.
This was conducted to help contextualize the participants' interpretation of the decimal odds, which could yield more realistic insights into perceived risks and betting behaviors.

text.text: Finally, the study explored the variables moderating the impact of the availability of cash-outs on key dependent behaviors (betting vs. no betting, amount of money wagered, odds associated with the bets).

To do this, three random forest models, which use multiple decision trees to predict an outcome, were conducted separately for each of these outcome variables, examining how various demographic and self-report variables influenced these betting behaviors.
Data were split into training and test sets in an 80-20 ratio, and the training set was used to find the number of variables sampled at each split of a decision tree for the random forest models.
The number of variables was set between 1 and the number of included interaction variables, and tuned via repeated 10-fold cross-validation.
To address class imbalance in the categorical outcomes, stratified bootstrap sampling was implemented within the random forest algorithm.
For each tree, equal numbers of observations were sampled from each outcome category based on the size of the minority class, minimizing bias toward the majority class.
More specifically, the random forest algorithms drew stratified bootstrap samples matching the size of the minority class for each tree, preventing the majority class from biasing the split criteria.

Model performance was optimized using the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (PR-AUC), and hyperparameters included setting mtry, which determines how many predictor variables were randomly sampled at each split, were tuned using cross-validation to maximize PR-AUC.
To evaluate the importance of the investigated variables in moderating the effect of cash-out availability, the relative importance scores of these variables was calculated.

The analysis included all of the following variables: psychological traits and gambling behaviors assessed through self-report measures of impulsiveness, problem gambling severity, gambling patterns, and numeracy.
Behavioral outcomes consisted of: (i) whether or not participants placed a bet, (ii) the amount they wagered, and (iii) the odds ratio of the bets placed.
Model 1 predicted whether participants would place a bet.
The optimal model (ntree = 500, mtry = 54) achieved a cross-validated PR-AUC of 0.83 (SD = 0.08).

This performance was lower than the No Information Rate (NIR) of 79.83%, indicating that the model did not improve (p = .999).
Cohen's kappa (κ = .093) indicated slight, near random agreement, and balanced accuracy was low (55.09%) suggesting limited discriminative performance.

A diagnostic breakdown showed that while the model yielded a sensitivity of identifying actual bets (76.84%), and demonstrated poor specificity for classifying participants who did not place a bet (33.33%).
These findings suggested that the demographics and generalizable predictive performance in distinguishing between participants who placed maximum bets and those who placed other bet amounts.

The present study's findings do not support the hypotheses (H1 to H3) that cash-out availability influenced the likelihood of betting, the amount wagered, or the riskiness of bets made in this experimental context.
However, 80% (N= 471) of the participants included in the analyses chose to place bets.
Moreover, 91.8% of them bet the maximum possible amount (2,300 HUF).
This observed ceiling effect likely reduced the sensitivity of the analyses to detect differences between experimental conditions, and provides a possible explanation for the null findings.
Several factors may have contributed to the ceiling effect.

Participants may not have treated the reward as equivalent to their own money, although the CAPTCHA reward was framed as money participants had personally earned to strengthen their sense of ownership over it.
But the reward did not constitute their full compensation of 6,000 HUF, which may have reinforced this perception.
Participants may instead have treated it as supplementary, reducing their sensitivity to potential losses.

This pattern is consistent with the 'house money effect' (Post et al., 2008; Thaler & Johnson, 1990), in which individuals treat experiment-provided funds as money they are already ahead on, discounting potential losses.

text.text: Prior familiarity with cash-out was widespread in the study sample.
Only 20 participants had no prior experience with the feature (3%).
Those with prior experience may have relied on existing beliefs or habitual strategies rather than responding to experimental manipulation.
To understand the ceiling effect, the study design was compared with Newall et al.
(2022), whose Experiment 3 used a similar protocol but did not produce a ceiling effect.
Four differences stand out.
First, the present study sample had higher PGSI scores (Ferris & Wynne, 2001) than either condition of Newall et al. (2022).

One possibility is that cash-out availability does not alter betting behavior in online sports betting contexts or that its effects depend on the characteristics of the betting environment.

For instance, Bennett et al. (2024) found that cash-out availability affected behavior in a card betting task suggesting that the context or the characteristics of the cash-out offer may have moderated the effect of cash-out availability.

text.text: Real-life sports betting may involve more established expectations, strategies, and prior experiences, particularly among experienced bettors.
The sports betting task used in the present study may therefore have weaker or more conditional effects than those observed in other gambling contexts.
The reality is further complicated by the fact that cash-out availability may have an effect in a situation on some outcomes but not on others.

The recent findings of Hayes et al. (2026) found that cash-out availability affected willingness to gamble in a simulated horse-race betting task but did not affect bet amounts or bet risk among participants who chose to gamble.

text.text: This pattern suggests that cash-out availability may influence the decision to participate in gambling without affecting the characteristics of the bet, such as bet risk and amount.

Another possibility behind the null findings involves the number of betting decisions participants were asked to make. Bennett et al. (2024) used repeated trials, and they found that the effect of cash-out on bet amount was initially small and increased over repeated bet decisions.

text.text: If cash-out effects develop habits in betting through repeated exposure, a singledecision paradigm such as the present one may have been insufficient to capture them.
This possibility also overlaps with the methodological differences of the current study from Newall et al. (2022), whose multi-bet design provided greater opportunity for habit formation.

text.text: Repeated exposure may therefore be an important condition under which the behavioral effects of cash-out become more apparent.

Additionally, drawing from Ngieng et al. (2026) where the authors suggested that cashout may appeal primarily to those with lower impulsivity and PGSI scores, raising the possibility that cash-out features could facilitate sport-betting involvement among relatively low-risk consumers.

(2026)</ref> where the authors suggested that cashout may appeal primarily to those with lower impulsivity and PGSI scores, raising the possibility that cash-out features could facilitate sport-betting involvement among relatively low-risk consumers.

text.text: If so, the experienced sports-betting sample in the present study may have been relatively insensitive to manipulation.

Participants with established betting habits may already have developed strategies for managing cash-out opportunities, reducing the likelihood that experimentally introducing or removing the feature would substantially alter their behavior.
Although the present study was not designed to test this moderation directly, these considerations highlight the importance of examining individual differences in future research.
Several limitations of the study should be considered.
The experimental paradigm offered strong internal validity but limited ecological validity.

Participants made betting decisions within a simulated environment using experiment-provided money to gamble, which does not fully capture real-world gambling contexts where personal financial consequences are more salient.

Although recruiting active online sports bettors was a strength for ecological relevance of the participant population, it might have simultaneously reduced the impact of the sensitivity of the experimental manipulation.
Participants were likely to be familiar with the feature and have their own experiences and interpretations of the feature that the present study's explanation could not override.

A notable proportion of participants failed the question assessing their understanding of the cash-out function, suggesting that participants' preexisting knowledge or interpretations of the feature may not have aligned with the experimental explanation.
Lastly, the present study was conducted with a Hungarian sample, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to gambling populations in other cultural or regulatory contexts.
Future research, focusing on these new forms of gambling problems (Czakó et al., 2025), could also address some of these limitations.
text.formatted: Future research, focusing on these new forms of gambling problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Czakó et al., 2025)</ref>, could also address some of these limitations.

text.text: For instance, studies could increase the perceived personal ownership towards betting stakes by allowing the use of participants' own money or incentive structures that are more directly tied to effort and performance.

Field experiments conducted in collaboration with gambling operators using behavioral data from real betting environments could provide an ecologically valid context across multiple dimensions by capturing repeated betting decisions, more realistic financial consequences, and naturally occurring interactions with cash-out.

Additionally, recruiting more diverse samples, including less experienced or lower-risk gamblers, could also help clarify whether observed effects are moderated by gambling-related characteristics such as experience with cash-outs and/or with sports betting, impulsivity, and problem gambling severity.

Finally, longitudinal designs where participants are introduced to the cash-out feature and their betting behaviors are tracked over time may provide insight into the long-term impact of the cash-out feature.
Overall, the present findings provide no empirical evidence that cash-out availability influences betting behavior in this experimental context.
However, the observed ceiling effect in betting decisions suggests that the task may have lacked sufficient sensitivity to detect subtle differences between the cash-out and no-cash-out conditions.

Consequently, these null findings should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that cash-out availability has no behavioral consistent with the possibility that the effects of cash-out depend on the betting context, prior experience, and individual differences in gambling-related characteristics.
This contrasts with theoretical accounts suggesting that cash-out features may increase perceived control and encourage greater risk-taking.

Further studies employing more ecologically valid designs such as conducting field experiments with providers and involving more diverse samples that include less experienced or lower-risk gamblers are needed to establish whether, for whom, and under what conditions do cash-out features influence gambling behavior.

Participants were categorized into four categories (i.e., no-risk, low-risk, moderate-risk, and problem gambler) according to the scoring guide of the PGSI, and the Helmert-coded 3 version of it was used in the regression analysis.
Gambling patterns: Based on Braverman and Shaffer's study (2012), the following four questions was asked to assess gambling patterns: (i) "How frequently do you engage in gambling activities?"
(Never; Once a month or less; 2-3 times a month; Once a week; Multiple times a week); (ii) "On average, how many bets do you place on a single gambling day?"
(None; 1-5 bets; 6-10 bets; 11-20 bets; More than 20 bets); (iii) "Over time, how would you describe your tendency regarding the amount of money you wager in gambling?"
(consistently decreasing; slightly decreasing; stable -neither increasing nor decreasing; slightly increasing; consistently increasing); and (iv) "To what degree does the amount you wager change?"
(consistent; somewhat variable; moderately variable; quite variable; highly variable).
The Helmert-coded version of all four responses was used individually in the regression analysis.
